planting.note: Plant bare-root or container roses in late winter or early spring in well-amended, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Camelot was bred by Swim & Weeks and introduced by Conard-Pyle (Star Roses) in 1964, valued for its coral-pink color and strong cutting stems.

directions: Plant in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Camelot bears large, high-centered, coral-pink double blooms carried singly or in small clusters atop long, sturdy stems well suited to cutting. The upright grandiflora habit, typically around 4 feet, makes it a good mid-to-back-of-border choice alongside other Queen Elizabeth-lineage grandifloras. It repeats reliably through the season with deadheading, though a regular fungicide program helps manage black spot in humid, rainy climates. Prune hard in late winter to encourage vigorous new growth.

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container roses in late winter or early spring in well-amended, well-drained soil in full sun; Pink Parfait was bred by Herbert Swim, introduced by Armstrong Nursery in 1960, and won the AARS award in 1961 for its disease resistance and reliable repeat bloom.

directions: Plant in well-drained, average to fertile soil in full sun; Pink Parfait produces medium-large double blooms with medium pink outer petals blending to a pale peach-orange center, carried in small clusters on a compact, bushy grandiflora frame. It is noted for unusually good foliage health and disease resistance for its era, holding up well against black spot in humid climates. Deadhead spent blooms to keep the repeat-flowering cycle going through summer and fall, and prune back hard each winter.

common_name: White Lightnin' Rose (Fragrant Ruffled White Grandiflora)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container roses in late winter or early spring in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; White Lightnin' was bred by Jack Christensen and Herbert Swim, introduced by Armstrong Roses in 1980, and won the AARS award in 1981 for its strong citrus fragrance and pure white, ruffled flowers.

directions: Plant in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; White Lightnin' carries large, ruffled, pure white double blooms with a strong, pronounced citrus fragrance, borne singly or in small clusters on an upright, vigorous grandiflora bush. It is one of the more reliably fragrant white roses from the grandiflora class and performs well as a cut flower. Deadhead through the season to sustain repeat bloom, watch for black spot in humid weather, and prune hard in late winter.

common_name: François Juranville Rose (Vigorous Salmon-Pink Wichurana Rambler)

planting.note: Plant container or bare-root roses in spring near a large arbor, pergola, or fence in well-drained soil in full sun; this 1906 Rene Barbier-bred wichurana rambler needs a substantial structure and room to spread its long, flexible canes.

directions: Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun against a large arbor, pergola, or fence capable of supporting long, flexible canes. François Juranville bears large, fully double, salmon-pink blooms with a moderate apple-like fragrance, produced in a single abundant flush in late spring to early summer on vigorous wichurana-rambler canes. Its glossy, disease-resistant foliage and pliable growth make it easy to train horizontally over arches or along fences, which encourages more flowering laterals. Prune only lightly after bloom to remove old or crowded canes, since it needs a couple of seasons to reach full size.

common_name: City of York Rose (Fragrant Creamy-White Tantau Climber)

planting.note: Plant container or bare-root roses in spring near a sturdy fence, wall, or pergola in well-drained soil in full sun; this German climber was bred by Mathias Tantau in 1939 and flowers mainly in one strong spring-to-summer flush.

directions: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun against a sturdy fence, wall, or pergola. City of York bears semi-double, creamy-white flowers with a moderate, sweet fragrance, set off by glossy, dark green, disease-resistant foliage typical of this German Tantau-bred climber. It blooms in one abundant flush with some scattered repeat later in the season, on vigorous canes well suited to covering a large structure. Train canes as horizontally as possible to maximize flowering shoots, and limit pruning to shaping and removing dead wood after the main bloom.

common_name: Climbing Devoniensis Rose (Magnolia Rose — Fragrant Climbing Tea Sport)

planting.note: Plant container or bare-root roses in spring near a fence, wall, or pergola in well-drained soil in full sun; this 1858 climbing sport of the tea rose Devoniensis is a long-favored heirloom climber in the Deep South and Gulf Coast.

directions: Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun against a fence, wall, or pergola. Nicknamed the Magnolia Rose, Climbing Devoniensis produces large, creamy white to blush, intensely fragrant double blooms repeatedly through the warm season, performing especially well in the heat and humidity of Gulf Coast and Deep South gardens where many modern roses struggle. As a tea-rose climbing sport it carries soft, slightly lax canes best tied to a support rather than left self-supporting. It is notably heat tolerant and holds up well with minimal spraying; prune lightly to shape and remove dead wood, since heavy pruning sacrifices bloom.

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container roses in spring in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Westerland was bred by Reimer Kordes and introduced in 1969, later winning Germany's ADR-Sorte award in 1974. It can be grown as a large freestanding shrub or trained as a short climbing pillar.

directions: Plant in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Westerland bears large, semi-double, apricot-orange blooms with a strong, spicy fragrance in repeated flushes through the growing season. Bred by Kordes in Germany, it is exceptionally vigorous and disease resistant, making it a reliable performer in hot, humid climates where many hybrid teas struggle. It can be grown as a large, dense freestanding shrub or trained with support as a short climbing pillar. Prune in late winter to control size and remove old or crossing canes.

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container roses in spring in well-drained, average to fertile soil in full sun; Sparrieshoop is a 1953 Reimer Kordes-bred German shrub rose named for the Kordes nursery town of Klein Offenseth-Sparrieshoop, valued for its vigor and large, simple flowers.

directions: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun; Sparrieshoop produces large, lightly fragrant, shell-pink, single to semi-double blooms with prominent golden stamens, borne in generous clusters over a long repeat-flowering season. This German Kordes-bred shrub is notably vigorous and disease resistant, tolerating heat and humidity better than many older shrub roses, and its arching canes can be trained as a short climber or pillar with support. Prune lightly in late winter to shape and remove old wood, leaving most of the framework intact to maximize bloom.
